title: Pipeline Parallelism
subtitle: Topic: Pipeline Parallelism · Subject: Distributed AI Training · Seven questions, distinct illustrated explanations and a PyTorch two-GPU example.

PIPELINE PARALLELISM · DISTRIBUTED AI TRAINING

Split model depth; overlap microbatches

Place layer groups on different GPUs and move small batches through consecutive stages.

questions.stem: What is Pipeline Parallelism in Distributed AI Training, and how does it divide a neural network across multiple GPUs?
options: Pipeline Parallelism divides a neural network into consecutive layer stages, but each GPU retains a complete copy of every layer. Microbatches reduce the number of examples processed without changing how model parameters are stored throughout training.

Pipeline Parallelism divides a neural network into consecutive groups of layers called stages, places those stages on different GPUs, and sends activations forward and gradients backward. Overlapping microbatches keeps stages working concurrently.

Pipeline Parallelism assigns layer groups to different GPUs and moves activations forward, but each stage trains its weights independently. Gradients never cross stage boundaries and the partial models are merged after training ends.

Pipeline Parallelism partitions the weight matrices inside every layer across GPUs, while keeping the complete sequence of layers on each device. Microbatches are combined only when the GPUs finish their separate computations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Pipeline Parallelism (PP) divides a deep neural network by layer groups. GPU 0 might execute the first layers, GPU 1 the middle layers, and GPU 2 the final layers. Forward activations travel to later stages; training gradients travel backward. By splitting a batch into microbatches, one stage can process the next input while another processes an earlier one. For example, a large image classifier can place its early, middle, and final blocks on separate accelerators. Each GPU stores its assigned stages, not a full copy of every layer.

questions.stem: How do microbatches make Pipeline Parallelism more efficient, and why can different GPUs work on separate microbatches at the same time?
options: Microbatching creates several copies of the same training examples and sends every copy through a separate full-model replica. GPUs work concurrently because each GPU independently contains every stage and all the original layers during execution on each iteration.

Microbatching divides a training batch among GPUs, but all stages process one microbatch simultaneously before moving to the next. Overlap comes from using fewer examples rather than concurrent work on different stage inputs.

Microbatching assigns a different set of neural-network layers to each training example. Multiple GPUs work at once because the examples skip stages they do not own, avoiding activation communication across pipeline boundaries and scheduling delays.

Microbatching splits a training batch into smaller pieces that flow through the same ordered stages. Once the pipeline fills, different GPUs process different microbatches concurrently, increasing overlap while leaving some startup and drain idle time.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a four-stage language model and four microbatches, M1–M4. At first, only stage 1 has work. After M1 advances, stage 1 can start M2 while stage 2 processes M1. Later, more stages are busy at the same time. This overlapping execution is why microbatches improve utilization. However, the pipeline still needs time to fill and drain, leaving some GPUs idle. A microbatch is a portion of the real batch, not a duplicated set of examples or a way to skip layers.

questions.stem: How is Pipeline Parallelism different from Data Parallelism and Tensor Parallelism, and why might a large training job combine all three?
options: Pipeline Parallelism assigns consecutive layer groups to different stages. Data Parallelism trains replicated model groups on separate batches, while Tensor Parallelism divides computations inside a layer. Combining them can distribute model depth, width, and data.

Pipeline Parallelism divides individual weight matrices, Data Parallelism assigns complete layer groups to stages, and Tensor Parallelism replicates the whole model across batches. Combining them distributes training, but each strategy divides a different component.

Pipeline Parallelism assigns complete layer groups to GPUs, Data Parallelism divides example batches across model replicas, and Tensor Parallelism keeps whole layers on different stages. Combining them increases replicas without sharding oversized weight matrices.

Pipeline Parallelism assigns layer groups to stages and Tensor Parallelism splits weights within layers, but Data Parallelism gives each GPU unrelated model parameters and never synchronizes updates. A combined job produces independently trained networks.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The three parallel strategies divide different dimensions. Pipeline Parallelism divides model depth into stage groups. Tensor Parallelism divides very large operations within a layer, such as a projection matrix. Data Parallelism creates training replicas that use different batches and coordinate gradients. For example, an image-generation model might use two GPUs per wide layer, four groups of layers as pipeline stages, and several data replicas. Combining the methods can fit larger networks and process more data, but the communication patterns must be coordinated.

questions.stem: During forward and backward training, what do pipeline stages exchange, and how do GPipe and 1F1B scheduling differ?
options: Stages send forward gradients and backward activations between GPUs during training. GPipe alternates one forward and backward pass from the start, while 1F1B completes all microbatch forwards before beginning any backward work.

Stages transfer activations forward and gradients backward, but GPipe only sends communication after every stage finishes a full training epoch. The 1F1B schedule removes all interstage communication by caching inputs on each GPU instead.

Stages send forward activations to later stages and backward gradients to earlier stages. GPipe runs the microbatch forwards before their backwards, while 1F1B alternates forward and backward tasks during steady-state pipeline execution.

Stages exchange forward activations and backward gradients, but GPipe requires each microbatch to finish its complete forward and backward cycle before another begins. A 1F1B schedule uses a single GPU for all backward passes.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In the forward pass, a stage sends its computed activations to the next stage. During backpropagation, the next stage sends activation gradients toward the earlier stage so both can train their local weights. GPipe uses a fill-and-drain approach: the scheduled forwards run before the backwards. A 1F1B schedule alternates a forward and a backward task during steady state, which can reduce the number of stored activations. For example, a speech model split across GPUs can use 1F1B to manage memory while several audio microbatches are in flight.

questions.stem: How can PyTorch use PipelineStage and ScheduleGPipe to divide a model across two GPUs and train it using microbatches?
options: Initialize distributed processes and wrap the entire complete model in PipelineStage on both GPUs. ScheduleGPipe then splits only the input batch, so each process trains all layers independently without transferring activations between stages or passing gradients backward.

Initialize distributed GPU processes, place consecutive model layers in separate stage modules, wrap each module with PipelineStage, and create ScheduleGPipe with a microbatch count and loss function. The schedule coordinates stage communication and training work.

Create separate stage modules and a ScheduleGPipe object, but call the schedule without initializing distributed communication. The scheduler discovers every remote GPU automatically and moves activations between unrelated processes without a process group or established connections.

Divide layers across two modules and initialize a process group, but use ScheduleGPipe only to collect final predictions. Each GPU must run forward and backward passes on the entire model because PipelineStage does not manage gradients.
questions.explanation: Explanation: PyTorch's pipelining API lets each distributed process own a model stage. `PipelineStage` wraps that local module; `ScheduleGPipe` divides a batch into microbatches and coordinates their order and communication. In a two-GPU example, the first process can own a Linear/ReLU block, while the second owns the output Linear layer. Provide a training loss so gradients can flow backward, then step each stage's optimizer. The compact code example illustrates the stage layout; real training also handles consistent inputs, optimizer resets, checkpoints, and an evolving PyTorch API.

questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Two-stage PyTorch example

PyTorch · two-stage GPipe15 lines
01 import os, torch
02 from torch import nn
03 from torch.distributed.pipelining import PipelineStage, ScheduleGPipe
04 torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl")
05 rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
06 device = torch.device("cuda", int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))
07 torch.cuda.set_device(device)
08 block = (nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8, 16), nn.ReLU())
09          if rank == 0 else nn.Linear(16, 4)).to(device)
10 stage = PipelineStage(block, rank, 2, device)
11 schedule = ScheduleGPipe(stage, 4, loss_fn=nn.MSELoss())
12 x = torch.randn(8, 8, device=device)
13 y = torch.randn(8, 4, device=device)
14 schedule.step(x) if rank == 0 else schedule.step(target=y)
15 torch.optim.SGD(block.parameters(), lr=0.01).step()

Two-GPU illustrative training step. Start with torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=2 demo.py. Real loops must reset gradients, synchronize data inputs, and manage checkpoints.

PipelineStage wraps each local block; ScheduleGPipe coordinates microbatch training.

questions.stem: What are pipeline bubbles and stage imbalance, and how can engineers tune microbatch count, layer placement, and communication for better GPU utilization?
options: Pipeline bubbles arise when microbatch examples contain repeated information, so increasing the number of GPUs always eliminates them. Stage boundaries should prioritize equal parameter counts, and runtime communication measurements are unnecessary after the model fits.

Pipeline bubbles are primarily optimizer errors caused by inconsistent gradient values between devices. Engineers fix them by synchronizing all weights after each layer, while layer placement and the number of microbatches have little effect.

Pipeline bubbles are idle intervals during startup and drain, but engineers should minimize microbatch count to keep every stage busy. Assigning the same number of layers per GPU always guarantees balanced computation, regardless of layer cost.

Pipeline bubbles are idle periods during pipeline filling, draining, or dependency waits. Uneven stage workloads also cause stalls. Balance stage computation and transfers, choose enough microbatches for overlap, and measure memory use, latency, and throughput.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A pipeline is not fully occupied when the first microbatch has not reached later stages or the last one is leaving. These idle slots are called bubbles. Uneven stages cause more waiting: a stage with costly attention layers may become the bottleneck. For example, dividing a transformer at equal layer counts may still leave one GPU overloaded by embeddings or output projection. Profile the stage times, rebalance boundaries, and try enough microbatches to overlap work. Watch activation memory and communication, since more microbatches are not automatically better.

questions.stem: How can Pipeline Parallelism be combined with Tensor and Data Parallelism for production LLM training, and what checks prevent incorrect gradients, stalled execution, or incomplete checkpoints?
options: Combine pipeline stages across layer groups, tensor sharding inside large layers, and data replicas for different batches. Verify collective ordering, gradient synchronization and scaling, shape compatibility, checkpoint restoration, memory limits, and measured training throughput.

Combine pipeline stages, tensor shards, and data replicas, but let each data replica update unrelated model weights without synchronizing gradients. Merge their checkpoints only after training, assuming this reproduces a single consistent distributed model with the same accuracy.

Combine the three parallel techniques by assigning each GPU a different stage and a full independent network copy. Correctness can be established solely from high GPU usage, without checking gradient parity, checkpoint shards, or communication order between processes.

Combine pipeline and tensor parallelism across layer groups, then broadcast input data without synchronizing data-replica gradients. As long as stage outputs have matching shapes, collective ordering and checkpoint completeness do not affect resumed training or numerical correctness.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Large language models can use pipeline groups to distribute depth, tensor shards to divide wide layers, and data replicas to process more examples. For example, a 32-GPU configuration could use PP=4, TP=2, and DP=4 when the framework supports that layout. Test against a smaller reference run: check loss and gradients, scaling conventions, collective ordering, and tensor shapes. Then verify a complete checkpoint can restore every shard and optimizer state. Monitor stage stalls, GPU memory, network time, and throughput. A job that runs quickly but trains the wrong model has failed.
